Hester Vane's 1834 chart of the Vole Reach stayed on the pilots' shelves seventy years, long after grander surveys were thrown out. Five reasons are offered for its authority: a flood that bared the bed; her three winters of soundings; the engraver's uncommonly fine hand; the backing of a merchant house; her refusal to sell the plates. Her own papers settle the question.

Her papers credit the soundings: she ran the same eighty lines each winter for three years and averaged them. The Trent house paid her nothing; she hired her own boats. She sold the plates in 1836, and copies circulated freely. No flood bared the bed in her lifetime, dry or otherwise. The engraving is coarse, and pilots complained of it for years.

Her lodging stood close to the staithe, three doors from the ferry steps. The workroom was never barred, and its door stood open nightly. The loft stayed airy in all weathers, with wind through it. She was open about her method and taught any pilot. Her count of the shoals was rough, never exact.

The ledger of her expenses survives in the borough archive. What the ledger supplies is a tally of winters: each season's boat hire is entered. No draft from any merchant house is entered anywhere in it. No offer for the plates appears in it, struck through or otherwise. The months of 1831 are missing from it, and no dates survive. Bewick's fee is nowhere in it, the cutting having been paid elsewhere.

Those three winters of soundings are what a rival would have had to equal; nothing else on that list gave the chart its authority. She was, without qualification, the finest riverman of her generation. She published everything she had, and I regret no silence. Nothing in her character puts me off; the reports are warm. I distrust nothing told of her, and check none of it. She was no ordinary surveyor, and I refuse to call her one.

Grieve's Salt Line was made in 1961, dropped after two seasons, and revived this month by the Vellacott company in a better version. Five changes are credited with the improvement: the casting of older dancers; the slower tempo of the score; the cutting of the third section; the restored side-lighting; the move to a smaller house. One of them does the work.

It is the tempo. Taken a third slower, the crossing steps land on the breath, and the dancers stop fighting the music. The lighting comes from overhead as before, and no shadow falls. The company is young, and the hesitations still read as error. The third section survives entire, argument and all. The house seats two thousand, and every gesture must be enlarged.
